verdict: REJECT as new material - already carried. concepts/rent-seeking.md has a dedicated subsection '### Where Talent Goes When Rent-Seeking Pays', cites the paper as Source 14 and links it to the Baumol page. No new page and no new sentence is warranted. Two small CORRECTIONS to that existing paragraph are recommended (see uncertainties): (a) the sentence beginning 'Their reading is that rent-seeking institutions do not merely waste talent, they retain it...' attributes a mechanism ('the most talented have reason to stay and compete for those returns') that the accessible abstract does not state - soften to the wiki's own inference ('one reading of the result is...') or cut; (b) optionally add that the rent-seeking proxy is a single component indicator averaged over 1995-2020 (endnotes 2-3), which is more precise than 'Fraser Institute Economic Freedom Index' alone.
claim_grade: B for the empirical claim (peer-reviewed journal article; observational panel, OLS and two-way fixed effects, no causal identification), abstract-level only. Source tier under 4c: Tier 1 on the peer-reviewed-academic criterion, but low-prominence authors and venue (Atlantic Economic Journal is a mid-ranked Springer journal; both authors are business-school faculty in the UAE with a small body of work on this topic, notably Facchini, Jaeck & Kratou 2024, European Journal of Political Economy 84). Use it as supporting a narrow empirical statement, not as a headline authority.

content_summary.authors_and_venue: Louis Jaeck, School of Business Administration, American University of Sharjah (ORCID 0000-0002-1952-1282; corresponding author); Hajer Kratou, College of Business Administration, Ajman University (ORCID 0000-0002-0354-3401). Atlantic Economic Journal, online 15 Sept 2026, pp. 1-23. JEL F22, J61, D72. Keywords: brain drain, income inequality, rent-seeking, allocation of talents. Data 'available upon request'. Reviewers thanked in the acknowledgements, so peer-reviewed.
content_summary.design_and_data: Per the abstract: panel of migrants from nine MENA countries to 20 developed destinations, 1995-2020; data from World Bank World Development Indicators and the Fraser Institute Economic Freedom index; estimators OLS and two-way fixed effects. Endnote 1 names the nine origins: Egypt, Djibouti, Algeria, Iran, Jordan, Mauritania, Morocco, Turkey, Tunisia. Brucker-Capuano-Marfouk (IAB brain-drain data) and Docquier-Marfouk are in the reference list as the likely migrant-stock sources; the body was not read, so the exact source is unconfirmed.
content_summary.rent_seeking_measure: Endnotes 2-3: the indicator is labelled '5Civ' (Fraser EFW area-5 style component) with data attributed to 'the V-Dem Varieties of Democracy (2026) dataset'; 'If nepotism, cronyism, and discrimination are widespread in the application of public administration, countries receive a lower score' (endnote 2). 'The value of the indicator rent-seeking is the mean for the period between 1995-2020' (endnote 3), i.e. a country-level time average. Endnote 4: the marginal effect of income inequality on high-skilled migration 'is evaluated using the mean of RS' (Figure 1). So rent-seeking enters as an interaction (inequality x RS), a cronyism/favoritism proxy, not a measure of rent size or of land rent.
content_summary.headline_finding: Abstract: 'when income inequalities are conditioned by rent-seeking institutions, there is a negative relationship between inequalities and high-skilled emigration, suggesting that unproductive inequalities reduce emigration.' Conclusion: 'Institutional reforms are thus needed to affect allocation of talents towards more productive careers.' No coefficients, standard errors or effect sizes were accessible.
content_summary.theory_lineage_from_references: Tullock 1967; Krueger 1974; Murphy-Shleifer-Vishny 1991 and 1993; Baumol 1990 and Baumol 2004 'On entrepreneurship, growth and rent-seeking: Henry George Updated' (The American Economist 48(1): 9-16, DOI 10.1177/056943450404800102); Mariani 2007 'Migration as an antidote to rent-seeking'; Del Rosal 2011 survey on measuring rent-seeking costs; Laband & Sophocleus 1988. The authors' companion paper is Facchini, Jaeck & Kratou 2024 (EJPE 84).
content_summary.relevance_to_georgism: Indirect: it is Tullock/Krueger-tradition rent-seeking (cronyism), not land rent; it does not mention land in anything accessible. Its only Georgist hook is the Baumol 2004 'Henry George Updated' citation.

existing_wiki_coverage: Full. concepts/rent-seeking.md (read): subsection 'Where Talent Goes When Rent-Seeking Pays' summarises the paper (nine MENA origins, 20 destinations, 1995-2020, WDI + Fraser data, OLS/TWFE, the quoted 'unproductive inequalities... negatively related to high-skilled emigration' and the institutional-reform conclusion), ties it to Baumol, and states the limits (observational, nine countries, Fraser priors); Source 14 gives DOI, 'abstract read in full', B-claim. The paper is not on concepts/rentier.md (the rentier page is about land/finance/IP income, and the paper has no bearing on it). research/baumol-unproductive-entrepreneurship.md and problems/rent-seeking-drags-growth.md carry the MSV/Baumol strand it builds on. No wiki page carries Facchini-Jaeck-Kratou 2024 or Baumol 2004.
uncertainties: 1. Body unread: every statement about mechanism, specification, robustness, sample counts and coefficient size is unverifiable here; the existing wiki paragraph's 'Their reading is that rent-seeking institutions... retain it' goes beyond the abstract and should be treated as unverified or re-labelled as the wiki's interpretation. 2. The sign result is counter-intuitive and rests on an interaction with a country-mean (time-invariant) RS; with country fixed effects the RS main effect cannot be separately identified - this is the wiki editor's inference from endnotes 3-4, not a statement by the authors, and could be wrong. 3. The abstract says 'data from the... Fraser Institute' while endnote 2 attributes the 5Civ series to V-Dem; the true construction is unclear (Fraser components are partly sourced from other surveys). 4. Paywall vs OA-metadata conflict: if the article really is CC BY, a T1 with a different network may be able to open the full text at link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11293-026-09861-7. 5. 'Brain drain' here is high-skilled emigration to developed countries, not a general emigration measure.
candidate_sources: William J. Baumol (2004), 'On entrepreneurship, growth and rent-seeking: Henry George Updated,' The American Economist 48(1): 9-16, DOI 10.1177/056943450404800102 - Tier 1 canonical-scholar paper with a Georgist title; not on the wiki (books/economics-of-henry-george.md mentions the title only). Murphy, Shleifer & Vishny (1991), QJE 106(2): 503-530 - already on the wiki (research/murphy-shleifer-vishny-allocation-talent.md per the Baumol page).
suggested_inbound_links: No new page. If the rent-seeking paragraph is corrected: concepts/rent-seeking.md (Source 14 annotation and the 'retain it' sentence).
Optional one-line cross-reference from research/baumol-unproductive-entrepreneurship.md (See Also) to the rent-seeking.md subsection.

title: Three Blind Assessors (Idan Rednaxus, Social Liberty, 29 September 2026)
what_was_fetched: FULL TEXT of the essay (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200; ~3,900 words) plus Social Liberty's home and About pages. Saved as rednaxus.html/.txt, sl_.html, sl_about.html.
verdict: REJECT. Tier 2 essay, AI-assisted by the author's own disclosure, that restates assessment material the wiki already holds from Tier 1 sources; no distinct, citable claim.
claim_grade: D (interpretive/policy essay; the factual relays are unsourced in the text). Tier 2 under 4c: Idan Rednaxus is a Social Liberty essayist with no stated credentials; Social Liberty is a newly formed California nonprofit (the Social Liberty Foundation; 'Education, not advocacy'; About page lists affiliations including Mises Institute and Libertarian Labyrinth). Not in sources/audit/people-tiers.json; the wiki has never cited social-liberty.org (grep). The essay ends with: 'The sentences themselves were drafted with AI assistance from that outline and then edited by hand.' Cite, if ever, only as origin of a stated position.
content_summary: An essay on assessment as a 'practice' (price without a sale, official claim, record over time) that moves from Domesday and CAMA/ratio studies, through why a land tax asks more of assessment than a property tax (land share is the base; residual, allocation, vacant sales, location surfaces; Somers' unit-foot system), to a capitalization argument (as the tax approaches full rent, sale prices fall toward zero, so a mature system must assess annual rental value, not price), an accuracy/stability/legitimacy trilemma resolved by smoothing the bill rather than freezing the roll, limits on automation (thin markets, land share, the capitalization trap, Zillow Offers' 2021 closure, Denmark's suspended valuations in 2013), a hybrid self-assessment idea, and a 'stewardship' proposal that assessment record land condition so owners' land improvements are exempt and degradation is a debt. Figures and cases are relayed without citation: IAAO COD 5-15 for single-family homes, Berry's regressivity finding, Cook County/ProPublica 2017, Pittsburgh's 2001 end, Prop 13, Estonia going two decades without a general revaluation.
existing_wiki_coverage: Nearly everything is covered from better sources: concepts/mass-appraisal-methods.md (ratio studies, COD/PRD/PRB from the IAAO standard, Berry 2021 regressivity, Gloudemans land/building split, residual and allocation methods, stale-roll failure mode, DALT as split-avoidance) and research/iaao-standards.md; objections/land-cannot-be-assessed.md; objections/lvt-destroys-its-own-tax-base.md already makes the capital-versus-rental-value point and notes land sales thin as the rate rises (lines 21-31); events/proposition-13.md; places/pittsburgh.md; concepts/harberger-tax.md and concepts/radical-markets.md for self-assessment; research/gwartney-estimating-land-values.md; Cook County in narratives/the-tax-you-cant-dodge.md. Not on the wiki: the William Somers unit-foot system by name (Somers appears on research/gaffney-georgist-city-growth-cases.md, people/tom-l-johnson.md and people/lawson-purdy.md only in passing), Zillow Offers as an AVM-failure example, Denmark's 2013 suspension of property valuations, and the 'land-condition ledger' idea. None of these is supported by a Tier 1 source in the essay.
uncertainties: The Denmark claim ('suspended its property valuations in 2013 after errors in the old system... replacement took years longer than planned') and the Estonia claim (no general revaluation from 2001 into the 2020s) are plausible but unsourced here; they should be checked against Danish Tax Agency / Rigsrevisionen reports and Estonian Land Board material before anyone uses them. The stewardship-ledger proposal is the essay's one original idea and is normative, untested and unsourced. No figure here is new.
candidate_sources: Danish Tax Agency (Skatteforvaltningen) and Rigsrevisionen reports on the property-valuation (ejendomsvurdering) system 2013-2020, for the Denmark assessment-failure case (BACKLOG candidate, not from this essay).
Estonian Land Board / Tiits (Lincoln Institute) for Estonia's revaluation history, already partly on places/estonia.md.
Zillow Group 2021 Q3 shareholder letter / SEC 10-Q for the Zillow Offers wind-down and inventory write-downs (primary for the one private-sector AVM example).

title: Essential Differences Between Transaction Tax and Property Tax (Alan Forester-Kaiser, Social Liberty, 10 October 2026)
what_was_fetched: FULL TEXT (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200; ~6,000 words incl. a 50-item source list). Saved as forester.html/.txt. Social Liberty identified from its About page (see item 2).
verdict: REJECT (borderline, one argument noted). A long Tier 2 essay whose empirical content is either historical narrative from standard sources or already on the wiki at higher tier; the single argument the wiki lacks (transaction taxes require a 'witness at every exchange', so they are surveillance-dependent, whereas a land tax needs no watching) is an unsourced interpretive claim by a blogger and not citable as support. If the editor overrides, the only defensible use is attribution as a proponent's argument.
claim_grade: D (interpretive/normative essay with historical illustrations). Tier 2 under 4c: Alan Forester-Kaiser is a Social Liberty essayist (no stated credentials; not in people-tiers.json); the essay closes with an AI-assistance disclosure ('Much of the research, the examples, and the sentences were drafted by an AI model working from that direction'). Its sources list names primary documents (Smith, Wealth of Nations V.2; Parker, The Dutch Revolt; US Supreme Court cases) but the text does not tie claims to them.
content_summary: The essay argues that a property tax attaches to the 'land agreement' (the community's forbearance and title-keeping, which Domesday, the Napoleonic cadastre and Torrens title show to be a service) and is a payback for value received, while a transaction tax inserts a third party between two people who gain from trading and gives them nothing for the charge. It lists effects (deadweight loss, compounding as in the Spanish alcabala per Adam Smith, no natural limit unlike a land tax bounded by rent, friction that grows as payments get faster), constitutional history (Stamp Act 1765, McCulloch v. Maryland, Grosjean, Murdock, Minneapolis Star; Proposition 13's reassessment-on-sale as a de facto transaction tax), the privacy argument (excises, the Fourth Amendment, Bank Secrecy Act, Miller/Smith/Carpenter, AI analysis of purchase records) and a taxonomy of transaction taxes (sales, VAT, gross receipts, excise, tariffs, stamp duty, transfer taxes, mansion taxes, Tobin and Swedish FTT, bank-debit taxes, payroll, capital gains, estate, licence, digital services taxes). Named facts: Toronto doubled its land transfer tax in 2008; New York mansion tax 1% over $1m since 1989; Los Angeles Measure ULA (2022) 4% over $5m and 5.5% over $10m on the whole price with collections below projection; UK Stamp Duty Reserve Tax 0.5% on share purchases; Sweden's equity-trade tax 1984-91; Brazil's CPMF 1997-2007. Working principles: tax what is held, not what is done; judge a tax by its trigger, not its name.
existing_wiki_coverage: The empirical core is held at Tier 1: research/han-ngai-sheedy-transaction-taxes-tenure.md (Toronto 2008 LTT natural experiment, deadweight loss 111% of revenue raised, explicitly framed as a reason to favour LVT); research/mirrlees-review.md (recommendation to abolish SDLT and replace the revenue with LVT/Housing Services Tax; line 53) and places/united-kingdom.md (SDLT and the 2026 reform debate; Resolution Foundation Home economics); events/proposition-13.md (lock-in); concepts/land-value-tax.md and concepts/canons-of-taxation.md for the benefit-principle and tax-base arguments; Smith's alcabala passage is in sources/publicdomain/wealth-of-nations.md. The 'land cannot be hidden' point is on concepts/mass-appraisal-methods.md. Not on the wiki: the surveillance/privacy comparison; the 'land agreement' framing as the justification for an annual charge; the Los Angeles Measure ULA example; Sweden's FTT.
uncertainties: Some facts look right but are unsourced in the text and unchecked here (ULA rates and revenue shortfall; Sweden's tax rates and repeal date; CPMF 0.38% rate). The surveillance claim mixes a legal-history argument with a predictive claim about AI-enabled enforcement; it is not tested by any study. The essay's use of 'property tax' for the recurring tax on held land glosses over that real-world property taxes also fall on buildings (the essay concedes this).
candidate_sources: Han, Ngai & Sheedy (2026), Review of Economic Studies, DOI 10.1093/restud/rdaf092 - already on the wiki; the right Tier 1 anchor for transaction-tax versus holding-tax claims.
IFS / Mirrlees Review, Tax by Design ch. 16 (Taxation of Land and Property) - already on the wiki for stamp duty.
Los Angeles Controller / City Administrative Officer reports on Measure ULA receipts versus projections (primary for the one US example not on the wiki).

what_was_fetched: FULL TEXT (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200; ~1,600 words). Saved as thompson.html/.txt. The petertheil.com scrape was not fetched.

content_summary: Explains Georgism and LVT (land monopoly, land banking, untaxed labour, community-created value), uses Alaska's Permanent Fund as the dividend example (says the latest payment was $1,200), argues LVT is resilient (land cannot leave town) and low-harm (supply fixed; no pass-through to tenants; quotes Friedman's 'least bad tax'), surveys Singapore (state owns ~90% of land, ~80% in HDB flats on 99-year leases), Hong Kong (land premium about a quarter of 2019-20 government revenue), Taiwan (low assessments kept the tax small) and Pittsburgh (Oates & Schwab: building activity above comparable cities in the 1980s, with the office-space shortage the main driver), lists caveats (honest assessors, cash-poor owners, losses to existing owners) and mitigations (phase-in, deferral), and recommends starting with a split rate.
existing_wiki_coverage: All of it: concepts/georgism.md, concepts/land-value-tax.md (including the 1978 Friedman interview, line 56), concepts/citizens-dividend.md and places/alaska.md, places/singapore.md (state owns about 90% of land), places/hong-kong.md and concepts/public-land-leasing.md, places/taiwan.md and concepts/land-value-increment-tax.md, places/pittsburgh.md and research/oates-schwab-pittsburgh.md, concepts/split-rate-taxation.md, objections/land-cannot-be-assessed.md. uncertainties: Alaska $1,200 and Hong Kong 'quarter of revenue' figures are unsourced in the post and unverified here. Thompson's statement that 'No country runs a pure land value tax' is a common simplification the wiki handles with more care (Estonia, Denmark, Jamaica, Johannesburg).

The post adds a Boldrin & Levine-based case against patent extension, sketches a rising levy on monopoly profits (from his earlier essay 'The Moat'), and gives an ATCOR primer tracing the idea to Locke (1691) and Gaffney. title: The Size and Scope of Commercial Property Tax Misvaluation (Troup Howard & Francis Wong, working paper dated 8 October 2026; SSRN 7585598, DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7585598, posted ~10 October 2026)
what_was_fetched: FULL TEXT READ (31 pp.). SSRN returned a Cloudflare challenge (403) to curl with browser and Googlebot UAs, to r.jina.ai and to WebFetch; Crossref gave the abstract and metadata (type 'preprint'); the paper's PDF is posted on Howard's research page (trouphoward.com/research.html -> uploads/.../howard_and_wong_-_the_size_and_scope_of_commercial_property_tax_misvaluation.pdf, HTTP 200, PDF dated 8 Oct 2026) and was parsed with pdftotext (saved as howard_wong_commercial.pdf/.txt). Page locators below are the printed page numbers. No NBER working-paper version was located: NBER's site search by title and by author names returned nothing for either (checked 2026-10-13). Correction to the queue note: the title page lists Howard at the University of Utah and Wong at LMU Munich (not Yale SOM); the earlier Wong NBER items found were w29306 and w32315 on other topics. The results use confidential Census microdata, so outsiders cannot replicate them.
verdict: NEW research/howard-wong-commercial-property-tax-misvaluation.md. Not an ENRICH: this is the first national, parcel-level measurement of commercial assessment accuracy; the wiki has no page on commercial assessment quality and the existing assessment pages (mass-appraisal-methods, iaao-standards, gloudemans, almy) are residential- or cross-country-framed. Suggested frontmatter: authors Troup Howard, Francis Wong; category research; subcategory wiki-research-assessment (or finance); tier Important; year 2026; source_url https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7585598; bears_on_objections land-cannot-be-assessed (cuts both ways, see below) and lvt-invites-assessment-corruption (evidence against appeals/capture as the main driver). Page must state plainly that the paper is a working paper, descriptive, does not separate land from improvements and excludes vacant parcels, so it is NOT evidence for or against land value assessment itself.
claim_grade: B (descriptive empirical work, high-quality national microdata; not peer-reviewed; no causal identification; correlations with firm characteristics rest on a 20,500-parcel matched subsample). Source tier under 4c: Tier 1 - Troup Howard (Assistant Professor, Eccles School of Business, University of Utah; PhD Berkeley; co-author of Avenancio-Leon & Howard, 'The Assessment Gap', QJE 137(3) 2022, already on the wiki) and Francis Wong (LMU Munich; a Berkeley PhD student and Lincoln Institute C. Lowell Harriss dissertation fellow on property-tax incidence in 2018-19 per Lincoln Institute and Berkeley listings) are recognised property-tax scholars with peer-reviewed track records on exactly this topic.

content_summary.data: BlackKnight (now ICE Mortgage Technology Property Data) tax-roll assessments and deed/transaction records, licensed pre-2023, sourced from local assessor and recorder records. Baseline sample: arm's-length transactions 2017-2019; about 121,000 commercial parcels and 3,995,000 single-family/townhome residential parcels across 900 counties (counties kept only with >=25 commercial and >=100 residential sales; figures rounded for Census disclosure). Excluded: multifamily, agricultural, vacant-coded and municipal-infrastructure parcels, fully exempt parcels, partial-interest/intra-family/nominal/multi-APN sales. Each sale in year t is paired with the pre-exemption assessment for tax year t. Out-of-sample check: 2020-2023 transactions. Firm link: exact address match of parcels to Census Longitudinal Business Database and Business Register establishments gives ~20,500 parcel-establishment matches. The state list is not enumerated (national, 900 counties); the ten non-split-roll states used for the class-rate comparison are CT, DE, IN, ME, NV, NJ, NH, OH, VT and WA.
content_summary.measure: 'Normalized assessment ratio' (NAR) = assessed value divided by the sale price, divided by the county-and-class median ratio (the 'local target ratio', recovered empirically), so NAR 1.1 means 10% overvaluation relative to the county norm; a uniform level shift is invisible by construction (appendix A.1.1), which is why the authors also compare effective tax rates. County-level 'relative error' = aggregate absolute commercial error / aggregate absolute residential error, each normalized by the size of its segment (equation 4; cf. PRD, but with a different interpretation).
headline_magnitudes: Dispersion: NAR interquartile range [0.77, 1.53] for commercial versus [0.941, 1.337] for residential (p.7): a quarter of commercial parcels are assessed more than 23% below sale price and a quarter more than 53% above. Pseudo-median NAR 1.094 commercial versus 1.114 residential; winsorized SD 1.105 versus 0.771; unwinsorized mean 5.28 versus 1.537 (Table A1, p.31).

Tails: 2% of residential parcels are assessed at more than 4.5 times the later sale price (p.6); a commercial parcel is 'more than two-and-a-half times more likely' to have NAR of 5 or more (p.7). Winsorization cap is about the 95th commercial pseudo-quantile, 4.95 (Table A1).

Commercial versus residential within county: of 900 counties only 80 (8.9%) show less aggregate error in commercial parcels; 60 (6.7%) show more than three times as much; median relative error 1.666, so aggregate commercial error is about 67% higher (abstract and text round to 66%); 75th percentile 2.13 (p.9, Table A1). 2020-2023 sample: median 1.653, 50 counties below 1 and 50 above 3 (Table A1). Share of parcels more than 50% off (NAR outside 0.5-1.5) is higher for commercial at nearly every level of residential error (Fig. 2B).

Regressivity by value: 'We find evidence of regressive patterns: lower-valued commercial properties exhibit systematically higher assessments' (p.2). Most extreme in the lowest price bins (below $75,000, Fig. 3A) and larger when value is measured within county (Fig. 3B), 'although a regressive trend is also evident across middle- and higher-valued properties' (p.10).

By neighbourhood: unlike residential (Avenancio-Leon & Howard 2022), little relationship with tract non-white share or income at the median; extreme over-assessment (90th and 75th pseudo-quantiles) is larger in the highest non-white-share tracts and in tracts with household income below $25-50k (pp.10-11). Valuations are higher in lower-density tracts (-0.012, p<0.01) and in tracts with more high-paying jobs (Table 1).

By owner/occupant type: no difference between single- and multi-establishment firms (Table 1 col. 3, coefficient 0.049, n.s.); law-firm-occupied parcels have higher, not lower, NAR (+0.362***) and real-estate-firm parcels +0.194 (10% level); NAR rises with employee count (0.020*). Industries with extreme tails (wholesale, transport and warehousing, information, finance, real estate, professional services, education, arts) stay about 3.5% higher even after outliers are dropped (Table 1, col. 1), which the authors read as unobserved heterogeneity assessors cannot see, not noise.
content_summary.revenue_and_incidence: Scale: US state and local property taxes exceed $650 billion a year on a $80 trillion base; commercial is 'nearly one-third' of real-estate value (p.1). Class-level medians barely move: nominal and effective median rates are similar for commercial and residential within county, and 'misvaluation, while large and widespread, is symmetric enough that it largely washes out of class-level medians' (p.14); pooled median effective rate 1.54% commercial versus 1.16% residential, which the authors attribute mainly to homestead exemptions and the geographic mix, not assessment error. So the cost is dispersion (horizontal inequity), not a systematic shift of burden between classes. Incidence: the assessment is a liability of the owner; the firm-level analysis 'implicitly assumes that at least some of the economic incidence... shifts onto tenant establishments' (triple-net leases pass it through); no pass-through estimate is made.
content_summary.explanations_tested: Supports the 'thin market / harder valuation problem' hypothesis (infrequent sales, unobserved tenant information, heavier use of the capitalization approach, which is 'much more common for commercial parcels', citing IAAO 2025). Finds 'little evidence' for appeals or regulatory capture: errors are right-skewed (more over- than under-assessment), larger and law/real-estate-firm-occupied parcels are not under-assessed, and commercial effective rates are not lower than residential within non-split-roll states. Key sentence, p.15: 'our results suggest that owner influence over the assessment process is not the first-order explanation for the national gap between commercial and residential accuracy.' Conclusion: 'additional expansion of government capacity may be necessary in order to ensure equitable tax treatment' and current practice is inconsistent with IAAO (2013) ratio-study uniformity standards.
content_summary.land_versus_improvements: The paper does not separate land from improvements, mentions no land value tax or site-value rating, and excludes vacant-coded parcels. 'Land' appears only in 'Lincoln Institute of Land Policy', 'land use codes' and 'agricultural land'. Any reading for LVT is therefore wiki analysis: the segment most relevant to a land tax (large downtown and commercial sites) is the one with the thinnest sales and the largest total-value errors, and the capitalization approach that fills the gap for commercial parcels is the same income logic land-residual methods use; the paper does not test land value error, so it neither confirms nor refutes the 'land can be assessed' response.

existing_wiki_coverage: No page on commercial assessment accuracy. Adjacent: research/bulloch-gaertner-hoopes-commercial-property-tax-microlocation.md (commercial property tax and business location; uses CoreLogic commercial records; mentions no assessment error); concepts/mass-appraisal-methods.md (ratio studies and PRD/PRB; Berry 2021 county r-squared 0.46 and regressivity; 'Because land is immobile and visible, gross mis-assessment is relatively easy to challenge' and 'land-value assessment errors are bounded and contestable' - claims that the commercial error pattern complicates for the commercial segment); research/iaao-standards.md (COD/PRD/PRB; vacant-land COD tolerance 5.0-25.0); research/almy-oecd-valuation-assessment.md ('~10% error floor' in high-quality systems; Howard & Wong cite a separate Almy Lincoln Institute paper on large commercial properties, not on the wiki); research/gloudemans-lvt-assessment-feasibility.md (residential, three jurisdictions, late-1990s data); objections/land-cannot-be-assessed.md; objections/lvt-invites-assessment-corruption.md (appeals and capture); research/holz-perez-truglia-simon-zentner-ai-tax-appeals.md and research/mccanless-property-tax-appeals-rentier.md (appeals asymmetries; Howard & Wong cite a different Holz-Novgorodsky-Simon negotiation paper and the Nathan-Perez-Truglia-Zentner appeals work, not the wiki's AI-chatbot experiment); narratives/land-and-the-black-white-wealth-gap.md (Avenancio-Leon & Howard 2022 assessment gap); narratives/the-tax-you-cant-dodge.md (valuation accuracy and the assessment gap). Berry (2021) regressivity is carried on mass-appraisal-methods.md and objections/public-choice-critique.md. Not on the wiki: Cornia & Slade 2006, Burge & Ihlanfeldt 2005, McMillen & Weber 2008, Amornsiripanitch 2020, McMillen & Singh 2026.
uncertainties: 1. Working paper, unreviewed, dated 8 October 2026; numbers may change (the footer still shows (c)2023). 2. Many quantities are 'pseudo-quantiles' with noise injected for Census disclosure, and counts are rounded; the exact winsorization cutoff is withheld. 3. NAR is relative to the county median, so a uniform class-level over- or under-assessment is invisible; the authors flag this and use effective rates as a check. 4. Sales-based NARs can be distorted by atypical sales (impairment, data errors, partial interests); the authors argue these cannot explain a commercial-specific excess but cannot rule them out parcel by parcel. 5. The firm analysis covers about 17% of the commercial sample (20,500 of ~121,000). 6. The abstract's '66% larger' versus the text's 67% (1.666 / 1.67) is rounding. 7. Sample is sales-selected: only parcels that sold in 2017-19. 8. No state list for the 900 counties, so state coverage cannot be stated.
candidate_sources: Howard & Wong PDF (author-hosted): https://www.trouphoward.com/uploads/1/2/7/7/127764736/howard_and_wong_-_the_size_and_scope_of_commercial_property_tax_misvaluation.pdf - the full text used here; cite SSRN 7585598 as the canonical record.

Avenancio-Leon & Howard (2022), 'The Assessment Gap: Racial Inequalities in Property Taxation,' QJE 137(3): 1383-1434 - already cited on narratives/land-and-the-black-white-wealth-gap.md; the residential counterpart.

Burge & Ihlanfeldt (2005), National Tax Journal 58(4): 723-740; McMillen & Weber (2008), 'Thin markets and property tax inequities,' NTJ 61(4): 653-671 - the thin-market mechanism.

content_summary: From the abstract only: the colonial zamindari, ryotwari and mahalwari revenue systems created different state-intermediary-cultivator relations; at independence concentration, insecure tenure, exploitative rents and fragmentation required agrarian reform. The Constitution used Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles (Articles 38 and 39(b)-(c)) and amendments: Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 generated litigation; the Constitution (First Amendment) Act 1951 introduced Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule. The study traces abolition of intermediaries, tenancy reform, ceilings, consolidation, tribal land protection, acquisition and rehabilitation, digital land records and the judiciary's balancing role, and concludes that amendments and judicial doctrines were central while implementation deficiencies limit effectiveness. No figures, case names or statistics appear in the abstract.
existing_wiki_coverage: None on Indian land reform or the constitutional history. The only land-reform case page is events/taiwan-land-reform-1950s.md and places/taiwan.md; Indian pages are land pooling (concepts/land-pooling.md), the Chennai property-tax RCT (research/duflo-hanna-olken-tandon-chennai-outsourcing.md), the Telangana CURE bill, and the 2024 mineral-royalty ruling. BACKLOG line 101 already records the gap and the Tier 1 anchors.
uncertainties: The body is unread: whether it cites Besley & Burgess, the Supreme Court cases or government statistics is unknown. The abstract is consistent with the primaries: Article 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule came from the First Amendment 1951 (Constitution text footnotes confirm Article 31B 'Ins. by' the 1951 Act; Article 31A, first inserted 1951, was recast by the Fourth Amendment 1955 and the Seventeenth Amendment 1964). The ceiling-specific proviso to Article 31A(1) and the state ceiling Acts listed in the Ninth Schedule (entries 21-64) date from the Seventeenth Amendment 1964, not the 1951 Amendment, so the abstract's 1951 account covers only the first step.
candidate_sources: Constitution of India, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice, text as on 1 May 2024 (PDF, 2.4 MB, https://cdnbbsr.s3waas.gov.in/s380537a945c7aaa788ccfcdf1b99b5d8f/uploads/2024/07/20240716890312078.pdf, read): Article 31A (with the second proviso: no acquisition of land 'held by a person under his personal cultivation... within the ceiling limit applicable to him' without market-value compensation - inserted by the Seventeenth Amendment 1964); Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule (284 entries as of 2024; footnote: 'Entries 21 to 64 and Explanation added by the Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964'); Article 300A (Forty-fourth Amendment 1978, s.34, w.e.f. 20-6-1979, replacing the Article 19(1)(f)/31 right to property). The legislative.gov.in landing page itself is JavaScript-rendered; use the s3waas PDF above or India Code.

Ninth Schedule entries that are ceiling Acts (read from the same PDF): 21 Andhra Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act 1961; 26 Bihar Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling Area and Acquisition of Surplus Land) Act 1961; 31 Gujarat Agricultural Lands Ceiling Act 1960; 34 Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act 1961; 41 Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act 1960; 46 Madras Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act 1961 (Madras Act LVIII of 1961) - the BACKLOG anchor, now Tamil Nadu. The Kerala Land Reforms Act 1963 (Kerala Act I of 1964) is entry 39.

Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (24 April 1973), AIR 1973 SC 1461, (1973) 4 SCC 225 - full text read at https://indiankanoon.org/doc/257876/. The petition challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Act 1963 as amended 1969 (para 2 of the lead opinion), and the Constitution text itself footnotes the case at Article 31C. Key for the basic-structure doctrine.

I.R. Coelho (Dead) by LRs v. State of Tamil Nadu (11 January 2007), (2007) 2 SCC 1, AIR 2007 SC 861 - nine-judge bench: laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to challenge on fundamental rights and basic structure. Described here from secondary summaries only; the indiankanoon.org document id was not located - retrieve before citing.
Earlier amendment-era cases to anchor: Shankari Prasad (1951), Sajjan Singh (1965), Golak Nath (1967) - all discussed in Kesavananda (read).

Besley & Burgess (2000), 'Land Reform, Poverty Reduction, and Growth: Evidence from India,' QJE 115(2): 389-430, DOI 10.1162/003355300554809 - bibliographic data confirmed via Crossref; abstract and full text NOT reachable (academic.oup.com is behind Cloudflare).
